The terminal-bijection argument applies to every completionLet  $P$  be the union of the three cores,  $Q$  its complement, and  $N$  any full auxiliary matching retaining  $A$  and  $C$ .In the tagged overlay of  $M$  and  $N$ , every vertex of  $P$  has degree two, with one edge of each matching, while every vertex of  $Q$  has degree one. Thus every open component is an alternating path with both endpoints in  $Q$ . Its first and last edges belong to  $N$ , so it has odd length and joins a white terminal to a black terminal.Consequently, these components define a bijection between the white and black vertices of  $Q$ . The white terminals are exactly  $T\cup\{W\}$ . In particular, any HH path ending in  $D$  would have to start at  $W=(4,5)$ ; there is no additional possibility of a black-to-black HH path.A direct coordinate check gives the stronger neighbourhood identity
$$\operatorname{Nbr}_{\mathrm{white}}(D)
=
F\;\dot\cup\;\{(3,10),(6,7)\},$$
where the two vertices outside  $F$  belong to  $P$ . Hence  $N_T(D)=F$ , as claimed.The retained paths assign the two distinct sources
$$(4,9),(5,8)\in F$$
to the centres  $(2,10),(6,6)$ , both outside  $D$ . At most six sources in  $F$  can therefore supply the seven endpoints in  $D$ . At least one terminal component ending in  $D$  must start in
$$(T\setminus F)\cup\{W\}.$$
This step does not prescribe the third centre’s component type.2. There is no HH path from  $W$  into  $D$ Deleting the vertices of  $A$  and  $C$  is legitimate because every other component must be vertex-disjoint from those retained paths.Starting at  $W=(4,5)$ , an alternating continuation through  $P$  can first reach only: $(3,4)$ , through the actual edge  $(3,5)--(3,4)$ ; $(5,6)$ , through the actual edge  $(5,5)--(5,6)$ .Within core 0, the possible continuing white states follow the cycle
$$(3,4)\longrightarrow(2,3)\longrightarrow(1,4)
\longrightarrow(2,5)\longrightarrow(3,4),$$
where each arrow represents a physical auxiliary step followed by an actual edge. Other exits from these states reach  $Q$  and terminate the component.At  $(5,6)$ , the black neighbours are precisely
$$(4,6),\quad(6,6),\quad(5,7),\quad(5,5).$$
The first is a  $Q$  terminal; the next two are occupied by  $C$ ; and the last is the preceding actual mate, which cannot provide a continuation of the open path.Thus your stated reachable-white set is exact:
$$S=\{(4,5),(3,4),(2,3),(1,4),(2,5),(5,6)\}.$$
It is disjoint from the complete white neighbourhood of  $D$ . Since an alternating terminal component cannot pass through an intermediate  $Q$  vertex, no HH component can end in  $D$ .The component forced by the pigeonhole argument therefore starts in  $T\setminus F$  and is TH.3. That incoming TH component needs at least two actual edgesA zero-actual-edge path would be a direct physical edge from its source to  $D$ . This is impossible for a source outside  $F$ .A path using exactly one actual edge would have the form
$$s\xrightarrow{N}b\xrightarrow{M}w\xrightarrow{N}d,
\qquad s\in T\setminus F,\quad d\in D.$$
The neighbourhood identity above leaves only
$$w=(3,10)\quad\text{or}\quad w=(6,7).$$
The second vertex is already occupied by  $C$ . For the first, its actual mate is  $b=(3,11)$ . The white neighbours of  $(3,11)$  are
$$(2,11),\quad(3,10),\quad(4,11).$$
The first two belong to  $P$ , so the only possible white  $Q$  source is  $(4,11)\in F$ , again a contradiction.Therefore the incoming TH component uses at least two actual edges. It is distinct from  $A$  and  $C$ , and the three components have disjoint actual-edge sets. With unit weights,
$$\operatorname{expense}_{TH}(N)\ge 1+1+2=4.$$
This proves the lower bound over all retaining completions.4.
